title: Narrating the Dark Night of the Soul: The Psychosocial Study of Low Point Stories.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Psychologists have long studied people's responses to adverse life events. Certain ways of telling a story of suffering, favored by a person's culture, may be more adaptive than others. The present study explores the culturally sanctioned script for how to tell the story of the lowest point in one's life.
METHOD: The present study introduces the Psycho-Social Script for Suffering (PSSS), a four-step narrative sequence through which a story of suffering features (1) situational context, (2) emotional expression, (3) closure, and (4) positive meaning. From a sample of 158 Black and white American midlife adults interviewed at three time points over 9 years, the authors coded 426 low point stories for the four narrative themes and analyzed their relationship to self-report measures.
RESULTS: Narrating low point stories with higher levels of PSSS was positively associated with measures of well-being, maturity, and adaptive personality traits. Moreover, with a significant main effect of time, PSSS increased over the 9 years as indicative of a developmental sequence in midlife.
CONCLUSIONS: The longitudinal analysis and rigorous mixed-methods approach offer novel insights into the potential benefits of narrating suffering in a way that resonates with culturally accepted discursive norms.
